module_title: Essential Knife Skills and Prep Techniques

lessons.title: Choosing and Maintaining Knives
lessons.body:
For street food, you need three knives: a chef's knife (20-25 cm), a paring knife (8-10 cm), and a serrated bread knife. In many African markets, you'll find locally made carbon steel knives from blacksmithsâthey're cheap, take a razor edge, but rust quickly. Stainless steel knives cost more but resist rust. If you can afford it, buy a Victorinox or similar brand; they last for years. Otherwise, a good carbon steel knife from a local smith is fineâjust dry it immediately after washing and rub with a little cooking oil.

Sharpening is not optional. A dull knife makes you work harder and is more likely to slip and cut you. Get a whetstone (1000/6000 grit) or a simple carbide pull-through sharpener. Use the whetstone weekly: soak it, then push the blade across at a 20-degree angle, 10 strokes per side. For daily touch-ups, use a honing rodâ5 strokes per side before each shift. If you can't find a whetstone, a smooth concrete step and water can work in a pinch, but be careful not to ruin the edge.

Store knives on a magnetic strip or in a wooden blockânever loose in a drawer where they bang against each other. Wash by hand with warm soapy water, dry immediately, and never put them in a dishwasher. For carbon steel, apply a thin coat of vegetable oil after drying. A knife that's well cared for will last years; a neglected one will be useless in months.

In high-volume street food, you'll cut through cases of tomatoes, onions, and peppers daily. Invest in a knife that feels comfortable in your hand. Test the balance: the knife should feel like an extension of your arm. If you have to squeeze hard, it's wrong. Also, consider a plastic cutting boardâwood can harbor bacteria, and plastic is easier to sanitize. Keep your board stable by placing a damp cloth underneath.

lessons.title: Basic Cuts: Dice, Julienne, Chiffonade
lessons.body:
Dice, julienne, and chiffonade are the three cuts you'll use every day. For a dice, first square off the vegetable: cut a thin slice off one side to create a flat surface, then lay it flat and cut into planks, then sticks, then cubes. For a medium dice (1 cm), cut planks 1 cm thick, then sticks 1 cm wide, then cubes. For onions, cut off the top, halve lengthwise, peel, then make horizontal cuts (parallel to the board) without cutting through the root, then vertical cuts, then slice across. This gives you even pieces that cook at the same rate.

Julienne means matchsticks, about 3 mm x 3 mm x 5 cm. First cut the vegetable into 5 cm lengths, then slice into 3 mm planks, then stack a few planks and cut into 3 mm sticks. This is perfect for stir-fries, salads, or garnishes. For carrots, peel first, then cut. For peppers, remove seeds and white pith, then slice into strips. Practice on carrots and cucumbersâthey're cheap and firm.

Chiffonade is for leafy herbs and greens: stack 3-4 leaves, roll them tightly like a cigar, then slice thinly across the roll. This gives you fine ribbons. Use it for basil, mint, spinach, or collard greens. For herbs like parsley or coriander, don't chiffonadeâjust chop roughly. Always use a sharp knife; a dull one bruises the leaves and turns them black.

In African street food, you'll often need diced onions, julienned carrots for garnish, and chiffonade of greens for soups. Speed comes with practice. Start slow and focus on uniformity. Uniform cuts ensure even cooking and professional presentation. A good test: after dicing an onion, all pieces should be roughly the same size. If some are big and some are tiny, your knife skills need work. Spend 10 minutes daily practicing on cheap vegetables like onions, carrots, and cabbage.

lessons.title: Speed Prepping for High Volume
lessons.body:
When you're selling 100 plates a day, speed is money. The key is organization: set up your station with everything you need within arm's reach. Keep a bowl for scraps, a container for prepped items, and your knife and board ready. Before you start cutting, group similar tasks: cut all onions first, then all tomatoes, then all peppers. This reduces switching time and keeps your board cleaner.

Use the 'claw' technique to protect your fingers: curl your fingertips under and use your knuckles to guide the knife. This lets you cut fast without looking at your fingers. For onions, cut off the top, halve, peel, then make radial cuts and slice. For tomatoes, use a serrated knife or a very sharp chef's knife; a dull knife will squash them. For peppers, cut off the top, slice in half, remove seeds, then stack and slice. For cabbage, quarter, remove core, then slice thinly.

Batch your prep. If you need 5 kg of onions, don't cut them one by one as orders come. Cut all 5 kg at once, store in a covered container in the fridge. Same for tomatoes, peppers, and greens. This saves time and ensures consistency. Use a large cutting board (at least 45 cm x 30 cm) so you have room. A plastic board is lighter and easier to clean. If you have a helper, divide tasks: one person cuts onions, another cuts tomatoes.

Invest in a few tools: a mandoline for slicing cucumbers and carrots (but watch your fingers), and a food processor for large batches of onions or cabbage. A food processor can dice 2 kg of onions in 30 seconds, but the pieces may be unevenâuse it for soups or stews, not for garnishes. For high-volume, also consider pre-cut vegetables from a supplier, but that costs more. Calculate: if you spend 2 hours cutting onions daily, and you pay yourself 500 KES per hour, that's 1000 KES. A food processor costs 10,000 KES and pays for itself in 10 days. Do the math for your situation.

lessons.title: Using a Mandoline and Food Processor
lessons.body:
A mandoline is a manual slicer with adjustable blades. It's perfect for thin, uniform slices of cucumbers, carrots, potatoes, and cabbage. The basic model costs 2,000-5,000 KES. Use the hand guardâmost mandoline injuries happen when people try to slice the last piece without it. Set the blade to 2-3 mm for cucumber slices, 1-2 mm for potato chips. For julienne, use the julienne blade attachment. Always cut on a stable surface; place a damp cloth under the mandoline. Clean immediately after useâstarchy vegetables like potatoes leave residue that rusts blades.

A food processor is a motorized appliance with interchangeable blades. The S-blade is for pureeing, chopping, and mixing. The slicing disc is for uniform slices. The shredding disc is for cheese and carrots. For high-volume street food, a 10-12 cup processor (about 15,000-25,000 KES) can save hours. Use it to chop onions for stews, shred cabbage for coleslaw, or puree tomatoes for sauce. But don't use it for garnishesâthe pieces are too irregular. Also, don't overprocess; pulse in short bursts to avoid turning vegetables into mush.

When using a food processor, cut vegetables into chunks that fit the feed tube. For onions, quarter them first. For cabbage, cut into wedges. For carrots, cut into 5 cm lengths. Feed them through the tube with the pusherânever use your fingers. The processor works best when the bowl is not more than 2/3 full. If you're processing a large batch, do it in batches. Clean the bowl and blades immediately; dried food is hard to remove. Most parts are dishwasher-safe, but check the manual.

In African markets, you can find used food processors at a fraction of the price. Check that the motor runs smoothly and all parts are included. A mandoline is cheaper and takes less space, but a food processor is more versatile. For a street food business, both are worth it if you do high volume. Start with a mandoline if your budget is tight, then add a food processor when you can. Always prioritize safety: never reach into the feed tube, and always use the pusher. Keep the blades sharp; dull blades require more force and are more dangerous.

lessons.title: Batch Preparation and Storage
lessons.body:
Batch preparation means cutting large quantities of vegetables at once and storing them properly. This saves time during service and ensures consistency. The key is to store each vegetable correctly to maintain freshness and safety. For onions, after cutting, store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days. They will smell strong, so keep them separate from other foods. For tomatoes, cut them fresh if possible; if you must pre-cut, store in a covered container in the fridge for up to 2 days. They lose flavor and become mushy quickly.

For leafy greens like spinach or collards, wash thoroughly, spin dry or pat with a clean cloth, then store in a container lined with paper towel to absorb moisture. They last 3-5 days. For carrots and peppers, cut and store in cold water in the fridgeâthis keeps them crisp for up to 5 days. Change the water daily. For potatoes, cut and store in cold water to prevent browning; use within 24 hours. For cabbage, shred and store in a zip-top bag with the air squeezed out; lasts up to 5 days.

Temperature control is critical. Your fridge should be at 4Â°C or below. Use a thermometer to check. Don't overload the fridge; cold air must circulate. Label containers with the date and contents. Use FIFO (first in, first out): use older items first. If you're prepping for a big event, do it the day before and keep everything cold. For street food, you may not have a large fridge. Consider a cooler box with ice packs. Change ice daily.

Safety: never mix raw and cooked foods. Use separate cutting boards: red for raw meat, green for vegetables, white for cooked foods. If you only have one board, wash it with hot soapy water between uses. Sanitize with a bleach solution (1 tablespoon bleach per 4 liters of water). Air dry. For storage containers, use food-grade plastic or glass. Avoid reusing containers that held chemicals. In hot African climates, food spoils fast. Keep prepped items in the shade, and don't leave them out for more than 2 hours. If in doubt, throw it outâfood poisoning will ruin your business.

lessons.title: Knife Safety and Injury Prevention
lessons.body:
Most knife injuries happen because of dull knives, wet hands, or careless handling. A sharp knife is safer because it cuts what you want, not what you don't. Always keep your knives sharp. Before you start cutting, make sure your hands and the knife handle are dry. A wet handle slips. Use a stable cutting boardâplace a damp cloth underneath to prevent sliding. Never cut toward yourself; always cut away from your body. Use the claw grip: curl your fingertips under and guide the knife with your knuckles. This protects your fingertips.

When carrying a knife, hold it by the handle with the blade pointing down and slightly away from your body. Never run with a knife. If you drop a knife, don't try to catch itâstep back and let it fall. When passing a knife to someone, lay it down on a surface and let them pick it up; don't hand it to them blade-first. When cleaning, never leave knives in a sink full of waterâyou might reach in and cut yourself. Wash one at a time, and dry immediately. Store knives in a block or on a magnetic strip, not loose in a drawer.

First aid for cuts: wash your hands, then apply pressure with a clean cloth. Elevate the wound. Once bleeding stops, clean with water and apply an antiseptic. Cover with a sterile bandage. If the cut is deep, go to a clinic. For minor cuts, you can continue working with a bandage and a glove. But if you're bleeding, don't handle foodâyou can contaminate it. Keep a first-aid kit in your stall: bandages, antiseptic, gloves, and a small bottle of clean water.

Prevention is better than cure. Wear cut-resistant gloves if you're doing high-volume slicing, especially with a mandoline. They cost 500-1,000 KES and can save you a finger. Don't cut when you're tired or distracted. Take breaks. If you're angry or rushed, you're more likely to get hurt. Also, keep your workspace tidyâclutter leads to accidents. Train your helpers on safety. A safe kitchen is a productive kitchen. Remember, a knife is a tool, not a toy. Respect it, and it will serve you well.

quiz.q: What is the recommended length for a chef's knife?
quiz.explanation: A chef's knife is typically 20-25 cm long, providing enough blade for most cutting tasks.

quiz.q: Which knife is best for cutting bread?
quiz.explanation: A serrated knife has a toothed edge that saws through bread without squashing it.

quiz.q: How often should you hone a knife with a honing rod?
quiz.explanation: Honing realigns the edge and should be done before each shift for best performance.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to store knives?
options: B) On a magnetic strip or in a block
C) In a sink full of water
quiz.explanation: Magnetic strips or blocks protect the blade and prevent accidents.

quiz.q: Why should you dry carbon steel knives immediately after washing?
quiz.explanation: Carbon steel rusts quickly when exposed to water.

quiz.q: What is a medium dice size?
quiz.explanation: A medium dice is typically 1 cm cubes.

quiz.q: What does julienne cut look like?
quiz.explanation: Julienne cuts are matchsticks about 3 mm x 3 mm x 5 cm.

quiz.q: How do you chiffonade leafy herbs?
options: B) Stack, roll, and slice thinly
quiz.explanation: Chiffonade involves stacking leaves, rolling them, and slicing into thin ribbons.

quiz.q: What is the first step when dicing an onion?
quiz.explanation: Cutting in half lengthwise provides a stable surface for further cuts.

quiz.q: Why is a sharp knife safer than a dull one?
options: B) It requires less pressure and is less likely to slip
quiz.explanation: A dull knife requires more force and can slip, causing cuts.

quiz.q: What is the 'claw' technique?
options: A) Holding the knife like a claw
B) Curling fingertips under and using knuckles to guide
C) Cutting with a sawing motion
quiz.explanation: The claw protects fingertips by keeping them curled away from the blade.

quiz.q: What is the best way to cut tomatoes?
options: B) With a serrated or very sharp knife
quiz.explanation: A sharp or serrated knife prevents squashing the tomato.

quiz.q: Why should you batch prep vegetables?
options: A) To save time during service
C) To make them last longer
quiz.explanation: Batch prepping reduces time spent cutting during busy service.

quiz.q: What is a good size for a cutting board for high-volume prep?
quiz.explanation: A large board (45x30 cm) provides ample space for efficient cutting.

quiz.q: How can you prevent a cutting board from sliding?
options: A) Place a damp cloth underneath
C) Hold it with one hand
D) Put it on a towel
quiz.explanation: A damp cloth creates friction and keeps the board stable.

quiz.q: What is a mandoline used for?
quiz.explanation: A mandoline slices vegetables into uniform thicknesses.

quiz.q: What safety feature should you always use with a mandoline?
quiz.explanation: The hand guard protects fingers from the blade.

quiz.q: What is the S-blade in a food processor used for?
quiz.explanation: The S-blade is for chopping, pureeing, and mixing.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overprocessing vegetables in a food processor?
options: D) It uses too much electricity
quiz.explanation: Overprocessing turns vegetables into a paste, ruining texture.

quiz.q: How should you store cut onions?
options: A) In an airtight container in the fridge
quiz.explanation: Airtight container in the fridge keeps onions fresh for up to 3 days.

quiz.q: How long can you store cut carrots in cold water in the fridge?
quiz.explanation: Cut carrots stored in cold water last up to 5 days if water is changed daily.

quiz.q: What is FIFO?
quiz.explanation: FIFO means using older items first to maintain freshness.

quiz.q: What is the recommended fridge temperature?
quiz.explanation: A fridge should be at 4Â°C or below to slow bacterial growth.

quiz.q: Why should you use separate cutting boards for raw meat and vegetables?
quiz.explanation: Separate boards prevent harmful bacteria from raw meat contaminating vegetables.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to carry a knife?
options: B) Blade pointing down and away
quiz.explanation: Carrying with blade down and away reduces injury risk.

quiz.q: What should you do if you drop a knife?
options: B) Step back and let it fall
C) Grab it by the handle
quiz.explanation: Never try to catch a falling knife; step back to avoid injury.

quiz.q: How should you pass a knife to someone?
options: B) Lay it down and let them pick it up
D) Hold it by the blade
quiz.explanation: Laying the knife down is the safest way to pass it.

quiz.q: What is the first step for a minor cut?
options: A) Apply pressure with a clean cloth
D) Put it under cold water
quiz.explanation: Applying pressure helps stop bleeding.

quiz.q: Why should you wear cut-resistant gloves?
options: B) To prevent cuts, especially with a mandoline
quiz.explanation: Cut-resistant gloves protect fingers from sharp blades.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are bleeding while handling food?
options: A) Continue working with a bandage
B) Stop handling food and treat the wound
C) Wear a glove over the cut
quiz.explanation: Bleeding can contaminate food; stop and treat the wound first.
